prize_parts.citation: for the proposal and realisation of optical lattice clocks, and their development to fractional uncertainties of 10^-18

statement.case_for: I keep B034 as a single-part prize. After reading all eight statements the scientific case seems to me unchanged, and the exchange has made it easier to state. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler and recoil effects for many neutral atoms at once, and Ye's group showed that this scheme can be controlled to the 10^-18 level, where blackbody, polarizability, multipole and lattice-light shifts all have to be understood at the same time. That is an atomic-structure and many-body problem, not only an engineering one, and I say this as someone who computes such shifts. The result does not depend on interpretation: clocks in several national laboratories agree with each other at this level, which is the strongest kind of confirmation a measurement can have. It has about two decades of development behind it. The credited pair maps onto proposal and realisation without forcing out a co-originator, which no other leading candidate can claim. I tighten the citation wording to 'proposal and realisation' and 'development', because round 1 showed that 'invention' invites the priority objection from other lattice-clock groups and I do not want the citation to claim more than the two names did. I do not rest the case on the redefinition of the second. It is supporting context and not a precondition.
statement.case_against: The reservations I took seriously in round 1 remain. Two earlier prizes sit close, the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for quantum control of single ions. Other groups (Lemonde, Ludlow, Lisdat, Bloom) have real claims to early lattice-clock demonstrations, so a two-name credit will be criticised however clean it looks. Eriksson's point that the clock is an instrument achievement and not a new regime of matter has weight, and the fundamental-physics results the clocks should enable (new bounds on constants, a redefined second) have not yet arrived. Finally, B028 has broader opening support, and I cannot exclude that my own proximity to precision atomic structure makes me read B034 more generously than a condensed-matter reader would.

responses.point: Pearce asked whether the neutrino-astronomy case looks stronger or weaker than theta13 on credit, in support of his B034 plus B005 two-part prize.
responses.response: On credit it looks weaker than theta13 to me, not stronger. Theta13 at least has three spokesperson names tied to three experiments, whereas B005 offers one name for a collaboration of hundreds, with AMANDA and the analysis leaders uncredited, and Kroll's question about who made the first statistically decisive observation has no answer in your statement. The diffuse flux is well established, but source identification is still developing, and Danielsson has said a single-name prize is too fragile this round. You also say yourself that the astroparticle part falls away if the credit cannot be justified. I take that as the answer, and I would keep the clock as a single part. I do not want to add a second subject to a clean prize and then defend a one-name credit in order to do it.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B028 first, says nothing forces the clocks to be decided this year, and treats B034 as the cleaner configuration if B028's credit is judged to misstate the original work.
responses.response: I accept your fallback logic and share it in the other direction: if the committee cannot agree on the B028 credit, I would rather see B028 awarded than have us split. But I do not think 'nothing forces the decision this year' favours B028. It applies equally to B028, whose theory has been settled for fifteen years or more. Neither is waiting on an event. My difference with you is the weight of the allocation problem. Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is a defensible trio, but the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal and the Fu-Kane-Mele and Moore-Balents three-dimensional theory cannot be credited, and the citation has to be worded to cover only the two-dimensional story. For B034 the credit gap is smaller and the physics is not contested. I do agree with you on breadth: topological classification reached further across fields than the clock will.

responses.point: Johansson asks whether Ye's frequency-comb work overlapping the 2005 prize weakens B034's novelty, and describes B034 as an advance in precision of an established technique.
responses.response: I answer the novelty point directly. The 2005 prize recognised the comb as a ruler for optical frequencies, and 2012 recognised control of single trapped ions. The lattice clock is neither. It is a different scheme, in which the magic-wavelength condition cancels the trap light shift so that many neutral atoms are interrogated at once without Doppler or recoil limits, and the credited contributions are the proposal and the strontium realisation, not the comb. I do not accept that this is only more precision of an established technique. A gain of several orders of magnitude from a new trapping principle opened a regime in which relativistic redshifts are measured across millimetres. I do grant that I weighed the 2016 prize overlap for B028 more heavily in round 1 than you do. Having read your argument, I would call that overlap a real but not decisive consideration: Z2 classification and protected edge states are not the same subject as phase transitions in the Thouless-Haldane-Kosterlitz sense.

responses.point: Eriksson regards B034 as an instrument achievement whose fundamental-physics payoff has not yet arrived, and ranks B046 first on a prediction-then-experiment arc.
responses.response: You are right that the payoff in new fundamental physics is still ahead, and that the clock is not a new phase of matter. I would put it differently: the criterion in the will is discovery or invention, and a measurement method that moved a whole field by orders of magnitude and is independently reproduced is an invention. I note that you now say you could be persuaded to recognise B028 first. I agree that B046 has the same prediction-then-experiment strength, but the credit problem is the worst of the three, with four names for three places, Andrei and Bistritzer both having claims, and Cao uncredited. Add roughly eight years of maturity and an unresolved pairing mechanism, and I would rank it behind both the clock and B028 this year. That is a judgement about timing, not about the quality of the physics.

responses.point: Mehlig says the clock's largest consequence, the redefinition of the second, has not happened, and that the 2005 overlap complicates the novelty claim.
responses.response: We agree that the redefinition should not carry the case. I have removed it from my citation and treat it only as context. Where I differ is the implication. If the redefinition is not decisive in either direction, the prize should be judged by what was demonstrated, and what was demonstrated is checkable: two uncertainty budgets at 10^-18 in separate laboratories, and clock comparisons that agree. You list B034 as the strongest precision-measurement option and as a fallback in your own ordering, which I take as a sign that the committee has more common ground here than the first-place counts show. I would ask you the same question I would ask myself: is the objection to B034 about merit, or about whether a measurement achievement belongs in the same ranking as a new class of matter?

responses.point: Kroll disclosed a doctoral research stay in the Hall laboratory environment and left recusal to the chair; the chair asks whether this requires recusal from the B034 discussion.
responses.response: I would keep my round-1 position: record it and let the committee weigh it, with one practical adjustment. Your link is a stay in a laboratory environment near Ye's, not a collaboration with Katori or Ye, which is a lesser tie than the shared-affiliation links others have disclosed. The better safeguard is that B034 should not depend on your vote. With Pearce and me supporting it independently of you, it does not, and I would prefer the committee to see that explicitly. If a vote is close and your ballot is decisive, I would want that stated openly in the record. I do not think full recusal is required, and I would not want it to be used by either side to move the outcome.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a two-name credit against the early claims of other lattice-clock groups, and whether 'proposal and realisation' is enough protection against the priority objection.
How much the 2005 and 2012 prizes should limit novelty; I judge the lattice scheme distinct but others on the committee do not agree.

Whether the clock's lack of a new fundamental-physics result yet is read as immaturity or as a reasonable stage for a measurement prize; I have not independently verified the current best uncertainty figures.

My fallback order is B028 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp first, then B046, but I rely on recalled history for priority in both fields and cannot settle the 2D versus 3D allocation from the supplied record.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: I have no documented personal or institutional tie to Katori or Ye. My documented collaborators are L'Huillier and the Lund attosecond group, the Keller group at ETH Zurich, Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti and Indelicato, none of whom are credited in B034, B028 or B046. I work in theoretical atomic physics, which gives subject proximity to the atomic-structure side of the clock, and that may bias me toward B034; I declare it for the committee to weigh. I have no stake in the candidates. On Kroll's disclosure I would handle it by transparency, not recusal. My earlier note that a general disclosure suffices stands.
